text:
My mother lives in a town with one stoplight, and for as long as I have been driving there it has been broken in the same way: green for a long time, then yellow, then red for what seems like a single second, then green again, so that you are always bracing for a stop that does not come. I took it at twenty miles an hour on a Saturday in late June, past the feed store and the Lutheran church and the diner that used to be a different diner, and turned onto Alder Street, where my mother stood at the end of her driveway in a straw hat, pretending she had not been waiting.

"You made good time," she said, though I hadn't told her when I would arrive.

"I left at six."

"Well, then." She looked at the car, and then at me, like a woman checking that both had come through intact. She is eighty-one. She has shrunk in the way the very old do, not evenly but in places, so that her shoulders sit below where I remember them and her hands seem to belong to a larger person. She smelled of sunscreen and, underneath, of the Pond's cold cream she has used since before I was born. I held her longer than she wanted, and she patted my back twice, the signal for release.

The house was the same: white with green shutters, one of two hundred like it, distinguished only by the garden, which fills the side yard and which my mother treats as an argument she is winning. Tomatoes staked with broom handles, a row of beans gone shaggy, zinnias in the colors of a child's drawing. A lawn chair stood in the middle of the grass for no reason I could see.

"I was sitting," she said, following my eyes.

"In the middle of the lawn."

"It's where the shade is at ten."

There was no shade there, only flat white sun on a yard that had not seen rain in nineteen days. I did not say so. There are two kinds of things to say to my mother, the kind that begin a conversation and the kind that begin a campaign, and I have always been a poor judge of which is which.

---

We had coffee at the yellow Formica table, its chrome edge worn to the color of a nickel where her forearms rest. She made it in a percolator that sounds like a small animal clearing its throat. Above the table hung the funeral home's calendar, which she uses, without irony, for the photographs of lighthouses.

"Doris Pruitt died," she said.

"I'm sorry. Was she the one with the—"

"The cats. No, that was Ida. Doris was the one whose husband sold insurance. Ida's going to outlive us all, out of spite."

This is how she gives me the news of the town: a ledger, the dead and the living entered in alternating lines, with no change in tone. I find it restful. I held the cup and let the names go by, the Hendersons' boy who had gone to prison and come back with a trade, the Methodist pastor who had left under a cloud no one would specify, the woman at the bank who had asked after me. "I said you were fine," my mother said. "You are fine, aren't you?"

"I'm fine."

"You look thin."

"I'm the same."

"You look thin in the face."

By eleven we had done the dishes, though there were only two cups, and she had washed hers twice. She showed me a pie plate from the church rummage sale, identical, she said, to one she'd owned in 1974 and broken in a fit of temper she did not elaborate on. She held it to the window, and the light made a pale ring on her cheek.

"You were in the doorway when I broke the other one. You were about six. You said, 'That's all right, Mommy, we have other plates.'"

"I don't remember that."

"No. I'm sure you don't." She set the plate down. "You were a very reasonable child. It worried me."

---

We ate lunch at one, because lunch is at one: tomato sandwiches on white bread, the tomatoes still warm from the vine, juice running to the wrist. She cut hers into four triangles and ate them in order, and watching her I remembered every summer of my life, the screen door, the radio in the window, the hush of a house in early afternoon when everyone in it was too hot to speak.

Afterward we played gin rummy with the cards she has had since I was in high school, soft as cloth, the queen of hearts missing a corner. She keeps score on the back of an envelope. She cheats a little, like someone long since forgiven for it, and I let her, and she knew I let her, and neither of us said so. Somewhere in the second game she looked at me over the fan of her cards.

"Do you ever think about your father?"

"Of course."

"I don't mean *think*. I mean, does he come up? Out of nowhere. You'll be doing something, and there he is."

"Sometimes."

"Yesterday I was hanging the wash and I thought, I'll tell Walter the line is sagging." She laid down a run of spades. "Twelve years. You'd think the habit would wear out."

"I don't think it does."

"No," she said. "I don't think so either." She drew a card, frowned at it, and the subject closed over like water.

At three I tried to persuade her inside, out of heat that had built into something you could lean on. The thermometer by the back door said ninety-six. She said she had a few things to do in the garden. I said I would help. She said I would only step on something. We compromised, as we do: she did what she wanted and I stood nearby holding a trowel.

She would not take the hat off, which I mention because later I had cause to think about it. The sun came down through the straw in a thousand little points and lay on her face like a rash. She pulled weeds. She tied up a tomato plant with a strip of nylon stocking, as she has all her life. At one point she put her hand flat against the small of her back and stood very still, and I said, "Mom?" and she said, "I'm looking at the light," and I looked, and it was only light.

---

At five I drove her to the diner, because she had decided it was a treat, and we sat in a booth by the window and she ordered the meat loaf and I ordered the meat loaf and she said I should have ordered something else. The waitress, a girl of about nineteen, called my mother "hon" and was called "dear" in return, in the voice my mother uses for those she is going to remember.

On the way back we passed the ball field and the water tower, its letters repainted so many times they've gone soft at the edges. She said, "Do you remember the night they lit the field for the first time? Your father brought a thermos." I did: the strange, flooded green of the grass, the moths going up into the lights like sparks. I was nine. I'd held a paper cup of cocoa with both hands.

"It was a good night," she said.

"It was."

"They don't light it anymore. Something with the wiring."

At the house I stayed until nearly dark. She walked me to the car, arms crossed, as though holding herself closed against a draft.

"Drive carefully. Call when you're in. Don't text. I don't like it."

"I will."

She put her hand on my cheek, briefly, the palm dry and warm. "You look thin," she said again, with great tenderness, and I laughed, and got in the car, and she stood in the driveway with the porch light behind her until the corner took her.

---

She went into the hospital eleven days later. A neighbor found her in the garden in mid-afternoon, sitting in the dirt between the bean rows with her hat beside her, answering questions in a pleasant, wandering way that frightened the neighbor more than anything. The heat index was a hundred and eight. By the time I got there she was sitting up, furious, in a gown of small blue diamonds, saying she had only meant to be out ten minutes.

She stayed two weeks at my cousin's and then, because she insisted, went home, and I returned a month after I'd left, to be there when the visiting nurse came.

The light at the center of town went through its odd pattern, and I braked for nothing. The house, when I let myself in with the key under the ceramic frog, had simply gone on holding the day I'd left it, like a held breath. The two cups were on the drainboard, upside down. On the table was the envelope with the score, her column longer than mine by eleven points, which was, I realized, a lie. The cards lay beside it, the queen of hearts on top.

Out back, the lawn chair still stood in the middle of the yard, canted now. The beans had split their pods; the tomatoes lay fermenting in the dirt, wasps working at them. Tied to a broom handle was a strip of nylon stocking, the cut end fluttering. On the hook by the door hung the straw hat. I took it down. Inside the band were a few of her hairs, white and very fine, and the faint smell of cold cream.

"You're letting the flies in," my mother said.

She stood in the hall in her housecoat, one hand on the wall, smaller than before, and also cross, and entirely herself. Her eyes went to the table, the envelope, the cards.

"I was winning," she said.

"You were not."

"Well. I'd have won the next one." She squared the cards with two fingers, and I saw her decide not to say it, and then say it anyway. "You look thin."

"Make the coffee," I said, and she laughed, and I filled the percolator at the sink, and the water ran cold over my wrists while behind me she began to deal.
